samples.hyp: To assess the necessary SARS-CoV-2 testing measures to prevent potential outbreaks in the Lusaka district of Zambia by focusing on asymptomatic individuals:
Research on the rapid reproductive system

The disease caused by the coronavirus (COVID-19), brought about by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa presents a significant proportion of asymptomatic cases (or cases with very mild symptoms) among individuals while spreading the disease.
The prevalence and extent of the disease in asymptomatic individuals are not well understood.
However, research indicates that addressing the disease is crucial for preventing the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a mathematical model called the "deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR)" to predict individuals at risk of being infected, in order to assess the impact on people with SARS-CoV-2 who are asymptomatic and to prevent outbreaks in the Lusaka district of Zambia.
We considered two scenarios; (1) assuming that asymptomatic individuals accounted for 70% of all those who contracted COVID-19, and (2) assuming that asymptomatic individuals accounted for 50%.

For comparison purposes, the model was evaluated by assuming that asymptomatic individuals also transmit, and that symptomatic individuals transmit more, and secondly, and more commonly, by assuming that the transmission by asymptomatic individuals is a fraction of that by symptomatic individuals.

Under the assumption that 70% of patients are asymptomatic, daily universal testing at a rate of ≥ 7911 tests per 100,000 people would be sufficient to prevent the disappearance of asymptomatic patients as a fraction of those who are infectious. However, if the same level of infectiousness was assumed, then a testing rate of ≥ 10028 tests per 100,000 people would be required.

About 50% of asymptomatic individuals with a minimum threshold of ≥ 4540 per 100,000 tested were sufficient to prevent the outbreak at the two levels considered for transmission among asymptomatic individuals compared to those showing symptoms.
Discussion and consultation

Our model suggests that identifying COVID-19 patients, including those who are asymptomatic, through mass vaccination can be used as a strategy to prevent the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, although it would be costly to implement.
Mass testing in large cities like Lusaka can reduce the spread of COVID-19, but is it feasible?

In 2020, computer models predicted that an effective way to prevent the spread of COVID-19 in large populations could be achieved through mass testing, followed by isolating those found to be infected.
However, the researchers stated that this approach may be very expensive and impractical.
In the early morning period, many people who were infected with COVID-19 did not show any symptoms of the disease but still transmitted it to others.

One study showed that between 50% to 80% of people with COVID-19 were asymptomatic (showed no symptoms) and that they could be responsible for 40% to 70% of the transmission to other individuals who contracted the disease.
The researchers wanted to determine whether identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help prevent the spread of COVID-19.
Similarly, they also wanted to know whether mass screening, meaning vaccinating people in a proactive manner, helps in identifying asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers developed a computer model that demonstrates how individuals transition from a state of being susceptible to infection, to becoming infected, then recovering, and finally becoming immune.
They completed the collection at the Lusaka cluster in Zambia, a section of officials including the international airport located at the border of two countries.

Due to the fact that COVID-19 symptoms appeared to vary from one location to another, they examined 4 scenarios, including COVID-19 patients where 50% or 70% were asymptomatic, while those patients were spreading the virus just like those showing symptoms or spreading to an intermediate level of those showing symptoms.
The researchers' model found that it was possible to prevent the spread of COVID-19 by conducting mass testing and isolating all individuals who tested positive, even if they were asymptomatic.
They estimated that in order to reduce the number of patients, which was above 90% in all conditions, 10% of the population in Lusaka needed to be vaccinated every day.
They also found that if we wanted to keep the number of COVID-19 cases stable, about 22% of the population needed to be tested every day.
Indeed, Zambia implemented preventive measures, yet the COVID-19 disease appeared to continue spreading.
Mass testing reduced the number of COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small town in Italy.
However, no research had been conducted to show that it could work elsewhere in a large city.
The researchers in this study did not conduct mass testing; however, they proposed a framework suggesting that mass testing could help prevent the spread of COVID-19 in large cities.
However, they warned that the method appears to be very costly.
They also suggested that it would be beneficial if this approach was combined with other measures such as lockdowns, contact tracing, and vaccination.
Zambian researchers also confirmed that asymptomatic COVID-19 patients appeared to be more prevalent in Africa at that time.
The estimation of low genetic diversity in African populations is due to the existing variations in genomes and regions.
African populations are significantly underrepresented in genomic research, yet they possess the greatest genetic diversity and experience numerous challenges globally.

Due to the lack of historical genomic prediction studies, we calculated the genetic variance to obtain polygenic risk scores (PRS) in analyses conducted across Africa and in datasets from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to better understand the overall predictive power of genomic research.
The accuracy of PRS increases as more genetic variants are discovered compared to research that shows inconsistent variants.
Among the citizens of South Africa of different ages and ethnicities, we find that the accuracy of PRS is low across all conditions but varies among different groups.
Differences in human ancestry in Africa significantly impact the accuracy of PRS compared to differences in other broad categories considered for people in the UK and Uganda.

We calculated PRS in African populations using genetic research focused solely on Europe and compared it with genetic research on different populations; the increased diversity resulted in greater accuracy benefits for the abundance of hemoglobin protein and the body's defense mechanisms against diseases, indicating a wide range of genetic variations known to cause sickle cell disease and subsequent malaria resistance.
The differences in the accuracy of PRS across African populations from different regions are as significant as the differences among populations outside Africa, necessitating equal consideration.
The reason why we cannot accurately predict hereditary diseases in people of African descent.
Researchers state that the methods used to predict whether a person will develop a hereditary disease or not do not work well for people of African descent.
This is because the data used for such predictions predominantly describe the genetics of people of European descent.

The GWAS repository refers to research conducted to identify genetic variations and diseases resulting from those variations, and scientists use it to investigate traits and diseases based on genetics.
They use GWAS to calculate an individual's risk of developing diseases or conditions based on their genetic makeup.
However, the majority of genetic data in GWAS comes from individuals of European descent.
In this study, the researchers aimed to assess how the calculation they use to estimate the risk of developing reproductive diseases using GWAS performs in individuals of African descent.
In another way, they also wanted to see if a more focused GWAS, containing sufficient data on African genomes, could enhance the generated hypotheses.
The calculation is scientifically known as a "polygenic risk score," or PRS.

They used computer models to estimate the genetic risk of developing reproductive diseases in Africans using GWAS, and also utilized medical records related to Africans to examine certain conditions or diseases that may result from genetic mutations.
Using a European GWAS, they found that the genetic markers for reproductive diseases were more prevalent in individuals of European descent compared to those of African descent.

They stated that signs of genetic diversity are widespread in parts of Africa because there is significant genetic variation among people, which is different from what we observe in people of European descent.
They further added that the accuracy of PRS increases as the frequency of the allele decreases.
The people of Ethiopia have more insights into genetic diseases due to their strong genetic similarity with people from Europe.
The inclusion of data from individuals of African descent in GWAS increases the accuracy of predictions.
The prediction of blood diseases was mostly accurate.

Previous research has shown that PRS is lower in African populations, meaning that the GWAS repository provides lower predictive power for the genetic predisposition of individuals of African descent to develop reproductive diseases.
However, we know that this is not true.

This research indicates that the low predictive power of polygenic risk scores (PRS) for reproductive diseases is due to the underrepresentation of African genomes in the GWAS database, resulting in current PRS being ineffective in predicting reproductive diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be more beneficial to use an expanded database containing genetic information from people of African descent.
Therefore, there is still work to be done to expand GWAS to include data from individuals of African descent so that we can better predict the risk of reproductive diseases in African populations.
The individuals who authored this research were from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
An Investigation into the Use of Eye and Brick Techniques in Combating Cervical Lesions and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
Approximately 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of contracting the human papilloma virus (HPV), which can lead to cervical cancer.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) combined with cryotherapy has been proven to be highly effective.
However, there is no information regarding the outcomes of cervical cancer screenings.
This research examined the use of visual inspection and Pap smear in combating cervical lesions and cervical cancer in Namibia.
Findings showed that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at a high risk of testing positive with VIA.
Older women, especially those with HIV, are highly expected to be diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
The visual inspection method appears to work well, although colposcopy for monitoring patients in Namibia should be improved and used for those found with HR-HPV.

They support screening that includes testing for HPV in people of different ages and in individuals at higher risk of developing cancer (for example, those with HIV, or conditions that compromise the immune system).

Emphasizing self-examination can be enhanced by implementing an initiative that includes using retrospective screening results, women's health objectives, new messages, and adapting to the country's circumstances.
Women in Namibia who are at risk of developing cervical cancer should be screened and treated early.
Many screening methods can indicate the risk of women developing cervical cancer, but in routine screenings in Namibia, these methods are not commonly used.
Researchers state that early screening and detection of warning signs can potentially save women from developing this dangerous disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the lower part of the uterus) kills many women around the world.
One of the leading causes of cervical cancer is the virus known as Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that affects the cervix, causing lesions, which can eventually lead to cancer.
Although the HPV vaccine is available, many women in African countries, including Namibia, cannot access it.
This means that screening for the virus or the lesions it causes is very important for these women, as it is the best way to help prevent cancer.
Researchers in this study state that therefore hospitals need accurate guidelines and information regarding better screening practices.
Additionally, healthcare providers also need to understand more about how factors such as age or health conditions can contribute to a woman contracting HPV and developing cancer.
They are examining some of the methods commonly used to detect HPV and lesions.
They also wanted to compare the examination, for example, removing bricks from a wall to check for cracks compared to searching for wounds.
They also wanted to determine whether differences among women, such as their age or having other diseases like HIV, affect their risk of acquiring HPV and cancer.
Understanding this information can help hospitals and clinics effectively implement screening procedures.
The researchers reviewed the medical records of 214 female patients who were screened and treated for HPV, lesions, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
The focus will be on early-stage cervical cancer, where the disease can be effectively treated.
They also collected data regarding each woman's age and their overall health status.

In reviewing these documents, it was discovered that different tests provided doctors with different information, and that they can be very useful whether HPV has not yet developed into cancer or has already developed.
For example, cancer was frequently observed in the collection and examination of breast tissue samples.
However, lesions were mostly detected and examined visually, using a technique called "visual inspection with acetic acid" (VIA).
The advantage of this method is that it enables doctors to detect wounds early and in a non-invasive manner.
This is because it uses simple, commonly used medical instruments for examining women's health, such as a speculum (an instrument used to look inside the vagina).
They also discovered that combining different methods provided doctors with more information regarding the risk of cervical cancer in women, especially when they were frequently screened.
Furthermore, researchers found that older women, especially those with HIV, were more likely to be diagnosed with cancer, therefore frequent screening is very important for them.
The researchers further noted that very few women were screened for HPV (before seeking treatment for lesions) despite the availability of screening methods.
Doing this could be an effective way to quickly detect this disease.

Overall, they stated that their findings indicated a need for the healthcare system in Namibia to develop more thoughtful strategies for preventing HPV and cervical cancer, using non-invasive methods that are effective in detecting these diseases as early as possible.
This research was conducted by scientists from Namibia in collaboration with those from South Africa.
The benefits of treating individuals with both HBV and HIV compared to those with only HBV in a cohort of people in South Africa.

In the global effort to eliminate the hepatitis B virus (HBV), we aimed to differentiate between individuals with only HBV and those with both HBV and HIV, to assess treatment efficacy and discuss ways to improve treatment.
We present our observations in a cohort of 115 adults with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
There were 39 (34%) patients who had both HIV and HBV.
We documented information on participants, financial aspects, and laboratory findings.

Compared to individuals with both HIV and HBV, those with only HBV were less likely to be HBeAg positive (p=0.01), less likely to have been vaccinated (p<0.0001), and less likely to be on antiretroviral therapy (p<0.0001); they were more likely to have detectable HBV DNA (p=0.04), and more likely to have signs of liver disease including severe thrombocytopenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and a high APRI score (p=0.02).
Three individuals developed hepatocellular carcinoma solely due to having HBV.

Our findings confirm that individuals with only HBV may face more challenges compared to those with both HIV and HBV, indicating a disparity in the likelihood of being referred to advanced healthcare facilities, monitoring, and treatment.
Researchers outline the guidelines to improve the treatment of hepatitis B.
In a previous study, researchers were able to demonstrate how having both HBV and HIV can facilitate treatment more than having HBV alone.
In sub-Saharan Africa, co-infection with HBV and HIV is a significant challenge.
Doctors need to understand how this virus and the medication used to treat it interact, in order to effectively diagnose and treat patients.
The researchers aimed to compare the outcomes of treatment in patients with only HBV, and those with both HBV and HIV.
In this study, the researchers worked with 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were discharged from Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients had HIV (39) while others had only HBV.
The researchers examined color, age, and size, and conducted various analyses in the field and in the laboratory.
It was found that patients with only HBV were less likely to be on antiviral treatment, showing symptoms of liver disease (since HBV is a marker that can lead to severe liver disease).

Researchers were able to demonstrate that individuals with only HBV had more difficulties compared to those with both HIV and HBV, because patients with both viruses were expected to be on HIV medication, which can also combat the HBV virus.

The results of this study indicate potential outcomes from the differences in providing more healthcare services, monitoring, and treating those with HBV compared to those with both HIV and HBV, with individuals having both HIV and HBV benefiting the most.
Researchers indicated that we need to improve and properly care for patients with only HBV.
One of the limitations of this research is the small sample size, as the study was conducted in only one country and within its healthcare system.
Some high-quality healthcare practices may present a perspective that contradicts the findings of this research.
Further research is needed to determine the exact differences identified in this study.
This paper demonstrated the power of collaboration, with researchers on this project coming from South Africa and the United Kingdom.
The inclusion of participants from South Africa in this research is important for the African population.
Moreover, this research could help develop better treatments for people with HBV, HIV, or both.
Examining the Impact of Instability on Women's Business Activities in the Local Government Area of SHIRORO, Niger State

This research examines instability and its impact on women's business activities in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing solely on issues related to women's economic empowerment, the common activities they engage in to create businesses, and the instability in their entrepreneurial endeavors.
A sample of 377 women was examined and the results showed that women in Shiroro are business initiators and are quite independent economically, mostly engaging in small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

The research also found that although instability affects women's efforts in starting businesses in terms of loss or reduction in startup capital and similar issues, the number of women starting businesses has not significantly decreased.

The research concluded that sustainable programs to improve women's access to and use of financial services need to be established, and local monitoring organizations should be set up and strengthened to prevent instability in the region.
Businesswomen in Niger need more protection.
Researchers found that women entrepreneurs in Niger are very innovative and economically independent, but security against criminals is a major concern.

The researchers aimed to understand the stability of women running businesses in the Local Government Area of Shiroro, Niger State, and how this stability affects their businesses and economic independence.
They interviewed 377 women in that area about the challenges they face in their work of starting businesses, financial independence, and instability.
They reported that 43% of women said they did not rely on men for financial support, while 32% said they had other people they depended on for financial matters.
Researchers also found that about 85% of women were earning money from various businesses, while very few others reported relying on a salary.
About 56% earned income from agriculture, while another 79% derived it from farming.
About 1 in 5 women earned money from hairdressing, tailoring, nail art, or laundry services.
The majority of women (91%) reported to the researchers that their businesses were affected due to fear of being attacked by thieves and criminals.
They lose money along with their husbands in such attacks, sometimes forcing them to care for their children without any assistance.
Those women also stated that they did not have enough skills and money to expand their businesses.
The researchers reported that despite these challenges, women in Niger continue to perform well in their businesses.
They stated that the Shiroro region was inhabited by people of different ethnicities and religions, and that this diversity was beneficial for business.
This research challenges the findings of other researchers who stated that women have less success in business because they are responsible for household care.
However, these researchers state that the success of women entrepreneurs in this region of Niger is mostly affected by attacks from criminals and thieves.
The researchers concluded that all stakeholders must come together to combat any challenges that may hinder business success.
For example, women in Niger need to have better access to financial resources, more productive farms, and greater stability.
They suggested that women in business could form groups that could help them combat thieves and criminals.
The micronutrients selenium, copper, and zinc during pregnancy are associated with the risk of preterm birth: A study conducted in Malawi.
Giving birth to a preterm baby occurs before 37 weeks of gestation.
The study was conducted to examine the relationship between selenium, copper, and zinc, and preterm birth.
This study included 181 women, with 90/181 (49.7%) having given birth to full-term babies and 91/181 (50.3%) having given birth to preterm babies.

The selenium level in the blood was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, copper was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and zinc was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L, with reference ranges of 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
The results indicate that there was no deficiency of selenium and zinc; and a high level of copper in the blood of pregnant women.
Preterm birth is associated with having high levels of copper and zinc in mothers.
Zinc, copper, and selenium are associated with preterm birth.
Researchers found high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who gave birth to premature babies, but they have not yet determined whether these high levels are due to the food they consume.
Giving birth to a preterm baby occurs when a woman delivers before the pregnancy reaches 37 weeks.
Giving birth to a premature baby can result in adverse health conditions for the child, including being born with disabilities and even death.
Preterm birth can be caused by various factors, but the role of many nutrients found in food and the surrounding environment is not well understood.
These nutrients are important for a child's growth, but researchers want to understand what happens if they are in excess.

In this study, the researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who gave birth to preterm infants, to determine whether giving birth to a preterm infant was caused by any of these nutrients being excessively high.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women who had given birth in two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital city of Malawi, between June 2016 and March 2017.
Blood samples were sent to a laboratory in Norway where the serum, which is the liquid part of the blood, was analyzed, and the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc were measured.
About half of the 181 women in the study were mothers of young children, and researchers found very high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.
Furthermore, they adjusted their calculations to consider many other factors such as age, health status, and pregnancy history to confirm that these nutrients contribute to preterm births.
They concluded that high levels of selenium and copper did not significantly contribute to preterm births, but high levels of zinc increased the likelihood of preterm births more than six times.
However, the high concentration of copper was a major concern for researchers, due to its known toxicity.
Having only 181 women participate in the study prevented researchers from accurately identifying the issues associated with high selenium levels, as the required sample size was 600.
The food consumed daily by the participants was not analyzed to determine the sources of these three nutrients, and neither the length nor the weight was obtained.
This is the first study to measure selenium, copper, and zinc levels in pregnant women in Malawi.

Africa is one of the continents with the highest rates of adolescent childbirths – over 18% compared to 5% in Western countries, therefore researchers want to understand if nutrition has an impact on this.
Home Range Behavior, Site Fidelity, and Habitat Preference of the Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals have behaviors of returning to a place and following times that help them in their lives.
Understanding the behaviors of that environment is very important in conservation and management, especially for species that are becoming extinct.

In this study, we tested whether the Pancake tortoise had the ability to return home when placed in a different location and also investigated site fidelity and homing in natural habitats in Kitui County, Kenya.
The behaviors of 39 turtles from 12 isolated remote locations were documented from July 2020 to June 2022 through radio tracking, camera trapping, direct observation, and note-taking.
Fourteen turtles were fitted with radio transmitters and relocated from their original habitats to different habitats away from their homes, and these locations and their behaviors were monitored.

Apart from only two turtles that successfully adapted to the new environment they were introduced to, all other turtles attempted to return to their original habitats, with 46.15% of them following the exact paths leading back to their homes, and 15.38% reaching areas believed to be near their homes.
The ability to return to their homes well indicates clearly that this is a species capable of returning to their homes.

The observation of the frogs' behavior in captivity showed that there was no significant statistical difference between the number of frogs that remained in captivity and the higher number recorded over the 162 selected days (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P >0.05), further confirming that this species has the ability to return home.
In another way, camera trapping in the immediate observation also showed that Pancake tortoises defend their territories, with males actively fighting off other males attempting to invade.
The missing pancake tortoises have an extraordinary natural ability to 'find their way home'.

Researchers conducted a fascinating study on the East African pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals can find their way back home after being transported a long distance from their original location.
Understanding the ways and reasons for doing so can be crucial in conserving these unique animals.
The behavior of nesting at home appears to be very important for these elusive animals.
To be able to return to similar habitats allows these animals to go back and feed, mate, and find shelter, all of which increase their chances of survival and reproduction.
Although homing behavior has been studied in marine and freshwater turtles, researchers in this study state that we know very little about the homing behavior of terrestrial turtles.
In this study, the researchers aimed to learn more about the behavior of pancake tortoises in their natural habitats in the arid regions of Kenya.
They observed the animals as they moved and fed, and also as they went to rest in the savannah, or in the thickets of the savannah.
Researchers monitored groups of pancake tortoises for almost two years and set up cameras to capture videos of them, but they remained elusive.
Similarly, they also placed radio transmitters on 14 turtles.
These small devices enable researchers to track the movement of animals, as well as monitor the locations where they spend their time during the day and night.
The researchers then took some of those turtles they had tracked and placed them in another location, to be able to study them more effectively.
However, what surprised the researchers was that two of these turtles started migrating back to where they were taken from, a distance of between 1 and 2.5 kilometers.
This prompted researchers to decide to try removing other turtles from their habitat to see if they would exhibit the same "homing" behavior.

It is surprising that nearly half of those that were relocated were able to find their way back home to the areas where they originally lived before being relocated, traveling a distance of more than 1.5 kilometers to get there.
Another 15% of the turtle parts were able to return to the same area, but they could not locate the exact spot where they were initially removed.
Researchers also discovered that different burrows almost had the same number of tortoises, indicating that tortoises tend to use the same places for resting.

Images captured by the camera showed that male tortoises were dominant in the territories, indicating that they were able to fend off other males that attempted to intrude into their territories or their ranges.

The researchers stated that this was the first time observing homing behavior in pancake tortoises, and the results indicated that these tortoises prefer to rest in the same locations whenever possible.
Their research did not explain how the turtles found their way back home, so future research in that area needs to focus on understanding this important issue.
Because some animals need to be relocated for their protection, this information can help wildlife conservationists ensure that tortoises are safe in their new habitat.
This research was conducted in collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, and it enhances our understanding of the migration patterns of turtles and other animals.
The Pharmacokinetics of High-Dose Oral Rifampicin Compared to Intravenous Administration in Patients with Tuberculous Meningitis:
Testing the Cultivation to Address Other Issues
High doses of rifampicin administered intravenously can improve outcomes in tuberculous meningitis but cannot be administered in settings with a high number of patients.

We hypothesized that the rifampicin exposure in the blood plasma would be similar between an oral dose of 35 mg/kg body weight and an intravenous dose of mg/kg, as these were the doses proposed in the clinical trial of this drug for tuberculous meningitis.
We conducted a study involving selected groups of participants on the behavioral opportunity of drug administration under the trial of high-dose anti-microbial therapy for tuberculous meningitis.
HIV-positive patients with tuberculous meningitis were recruited from hospitals in South Africa and randomly assigned to three groups with different doses of rifampicin:
oral (10 mg/kg), high dose (oral 35 mg/kg), and intravenous (20 mg/kg).
The behavioral sample was collected on the third day.
The findings were explained using noncompartmental analysis, and drug absorption was compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Samples of drug behavior were taken from forty-six participants (regular dose, n = 17; high oral dose, n = 15; intravenous, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The geometric mean area of rifampicin under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0–24) was 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) at the standard dose, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) at the high oral dose, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) at the intravenous dose.

The AUC0–24 GMR of rifampicin was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21) while the maximum concentration in blood (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for the higher oral dose compared to the intravenous dose.
The AUC0–24 of rifampicin in plasma was higher after an oral dose of 35 mg/kg compared to the intravenous dose of 20 mg/kg in the initial days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The findings support the oral dose of rifampicin in the preliminary trial of tuberculous meningitis.
High-dose rifampicin can be tested on HIV patients with TB meningitis.
Researchers confirmed that it is beneficial to start testing whether higher doses of the drug rifampicin can save HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis.
Three out of every five patients with HIV who also develop tuberculosis meningitis die from this disease that attacks the immune system.
Survivors often remain with permanent injuries to the nervous system and significant cognitive impairments resulting from brain damage.
This can affect their thoughts and behavior.
Some patients experience numbness or tingling, or parts of the face or body become numb.
Rifampicin, a powerful antibiotic used for tuberculosis, is often administered in capsule form to attempt to kill the bacteria causing tuberculosis meningitis.
Patients who are very sick often have difficulty swallowing these pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously in a drip form.
A needle is inserted into the patient's vein and the fluid can be injected into the body.
No studies had been conducted to determine how the patient's body absorbs this drug when this method was used.
Intravenous medication requires additional equipment, a bed, and a trained healthcare professional who knows how to accurately insert the needle into the vein.
Therefore, this is not something that can be done in underdeveloped regions of the world.
Doctors know that rifampicin does not penetrate well into the cerebrospinal fluid, the bladder, and the prostate, where bacteria can hide.
This is why higher doses are needed to completely eliminate all bacteria in the patient's body.
However, the researchers were not certain about how the higher dose could be effective and yet not harmful.

Therefore, researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom aimed to determine, using a small number of patients, whether it is safe to administer high doses of rifampicin either as capsules or intravenously, and how their bodies would absorb each dose.
It is important to know this as other researchers have not yet started conducting extensive tests or examinations, where they plan to administer higher doses of rifampicin to many other patients.
One of the three types of rifampicin was administered to 46 HIV patients in South Africa with tuberculous meningitis.
The first was a regular capsule medication given to patients at this time, containing 10mg of rifampicin per kilogram of the patient's body weight.
Another group received a higher dose of 35 milligrams per kilogram of the patient's body weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram of the patient.
Blood samples were taken from patients after three days.
The researchers measured the concentration of rifampicin in their blood plasma.
Rifampicin concentration was found to be higher in the bodies of patients who received high-dose capsules compared to those who received intravenous doses or regular doses.
The concentration of the drug in the blood plasma was the same in the high dose and the intravenous drug.
The medication was more effective compared to patients who only received the regular dose.
According to the researchers, this indicates that the health of patients with tuberculosis meningitis can improve if they receive higher doses of rifampicin.
It does not matter whether they receive it as a pill or through injection – the important thing is that they receive high doses, because now their bodies can store the medication effectively.
The results support the findings from tests conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
For example, two small-scale trials conducted in Indonesia indicated that the lives of many other patients could be saved if they were given high doses of rifampicin either orally or intravenously.
Unfortunately, researchers warn that the participants in this study were fewer than expected, which could affect the findings.
The research was conducted in South Africa.
Supporting the initiative to conduct a study to determine whether administering high doses of rifampicin to HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis is beneficial.
It is expected that this type of treatment will save the lives of many people in Africa and other places in the world where tuberculosis meningitis is a major problem.
Can the use of compost and organic matter improve the quality of rocky soil found near the seashore?
Soil degradation is a significant threat to agriculture in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Many authors have highlighted the benefits of using organic matter and compost in soil fertilization.

In this study, a 30-day incubation experiment was conducted with each treatment containing 120 g of rice husks, coconut husks (coco300 and coco700), or bird droppings compost; and compost of rice husks or compost of coconut husks, each amended with a 1% proportion (cococomp) and soil.

Further research involved compost made from bird droppings and rice husk ash (1% compost + 1% ash: 1% soil) to investigate their effects on soil moisture, soil pH; soil microbial carbon, total nitrogen gas, and available nitrogen distribution.
Organic matter and compost, whether used alone or in combination with organic compost, increased the soil pH by 0.28-2.29 units compared to untreated soil.

The initial yield from compost alone/rice husk compost/legume residues or a mixture of legume residues and compost was higher than the non-mixed ones, similar to that obtained from legume residues alone.

Key components in explaining intensive care include the detection, monitoring, and treatment of critical illnesses; support for vital functions; primary and specialized care; comprehensive management of critical illnesses; and the involvement of specialized healthcare professionals and equipment.

The definition we proposed for a severe disease is, "a condition characterized by the failure of a vital organ, a significant risk of rapid death if treatment is not provided, along with the potential for recovery."
The proposed description of intensive care is, "detecting, monitoring, and treating patients with severe illnesses by initiating and continuously supporting the function of vital body systems."
Definitions of severe disease and intensive care lack consensus and are used in different ways.

Researchers are tracking how coronavirus variants mutate to better understand how vaccines work on different virus strains.
Covid-19 has killed many people worldwide.
In a process known as genomic surveillance, scientists track how the virus's genome and proteins change as the virus spreads.
They use that information to address the disease and guide the development of the vaccine.
For example, by understanding the structure of the virus protein, researchers can develop a vaccine targeting those proteins to help prevent the virus from entering human cells.
In this study, the researchers specifically examined how the SARS-CoV-2 virus had mutated in Uganda.
Researchers observed the genetic makeup of the virus in samples containing COVID-19 across Uganda.
They used computer software to track the lineage of the newly discovered virus (called A.23.1), and they were able to see how this virus connects in the lineage with the ancestors of SARS-CoV-2.
Other findings indicate that A.23.1 originated from the lineage A.23, and was detected in samples with a prevalence of 90%.
In other words, it was a subset of samples from Uganda starting from October 2020.
They also discovered that the A.23.1 variant had many mutations in the spike protein similar to those observed in other mentioned variants.
These mutations suggest that the variant is more transmissible and resistant to vaccines and other treatments.
This research enhances the effort to sequence SARS-CoV-2 variants globally.
The findings add to the growing body of evidence indicating that SARS-CoV-2 is rapidly mutating as it spreads and infects a large number of people, while also evading vaccine-induced immunity.
However, further research is needed to understand the actual impact and function of the spike protein mutation in A.23.1.
Researchers recommend further monitoring of the genetic makeup to help understand how virus strains are affected by the available medication in Uganda and other countries.
They also state that monitoring human movement globally is crucial as it enables researchers to better understand how the virus spreads in a particular region.
What does a woman do?
The research highlights the factors and conditions leading to female circumcision in the countries of Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.
Female genital mutilation is a harmful traditional practice that violates women's rights and has negative health consequences.
This paper highlights the reasons and circumstances leading to female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) in certain regions found in three countries – Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.

The data was collected through surveys administered to young people (aged 15-24) in households and through focus group discussions, interviewing young people as well as key informants in the community in the years 2016 and 2017.
Analyses involving both descriptive and inferential statistics were conducted based on the main themes.

The findings from the research confirm some of the causes of FGM/C that were highlighted in previous studies, indicating that these causes have a strong correlation, and that cultural traditions are the main contributors to this practice.
In all three countries, these factors lead to the modification of women's bodies to achieve an ideal body shape according to cultural traditions, which is accepted in a system controlled by men.
This results in having a "sacred body" in the country of Indonesia, a "calm body" in the country of Ethiopia, and a "main body" in the country of Kenya.
Health workers and parents play a crucial role in decision-making regarding FGM/C in all regions.
In Kenya, young girls discuss their role in decision-making regarding FGM/C because they are considered mature at the time the circumcision is performed.

The research highlights how legal and socio-cultural changes in each region have led to shifts in the practice of FGM/C, resulting in the medicalization of FGM/C in Indonesia, a reduction in the age of girls undergoing the procedure in Kenya, and an increase in the practice of FGM/C in Ethiopia.
The three scenarios highlight a significant difference in the practice of FGM/C and what it means for young girls regarding the parts of their bodies involved.
There is a need to further explore the role of parents in decision-making.

Due to the complex interplay of factors leading to FGM/C in each region, research suggests that context-specific approaches need to be employed in all interventions aimed at facilitating sustainable change.
To end female genital mutilation, we first need to understand the reasons why it is practiced.
Female genital mutilation, a practice where parts of the female genitalia are cut or removed, is still performed illegally or under coercion in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.

Researchers state that understanding the reasons why it is practiced is crucial in helping to end this painful tradition, as well as preventing the health and psychological issues women experience as a result of this practice.
In parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), often referred to as 'female circumcision,' is still widely practiced.

Many people hold the misconception that FGM is necessary to maintain cleanliness or to keep women modest (not being overly self-confident and being calm), as well as to ensure that they will be able to bear children.
FGM is not necessary to achieve any of these according to scientific evidence.

However, in many cases, children who undergo FGM end up experiencing health complications later in life, such as contracting harmful infections, difficulties in childbirth, as well as other neurological issues.
Due to being a very dangerous practice and violating women's rights, many countries have banned it, but people still practice it secretly.
In this research, the investigators aimed to further understand the reasons behind the practice of FGM in different countries, and what beliefs people hold regarding this practice.
Therefore, they collected data on FGM in the countries of Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.

In each country, researchers spoke with people about the practice, including parents, young children, traditional leaders, health workers, and 'cutters' (older women who performed FGM on young girls).
In some cases, these individuals were asked questions individually, but they also spoke with groups of people, including young people and teenagers who had undergone FGM.
Researchers found that the reasons for FGM, the way it was practiced, and the beliefs people held about the practice varied in each country.
In another way, they also found that many people still use it, including in places where it is not allowed.

For example, in the country of Indonesia, traditional practitioners used a knife or needle to cut a part of the female genitalia (the part that stimulates sexual desire in women) when the child reached 40 days old.
People considered this as helping to 'remove impurities' and it was also important for religious reasons.
In the country of Ethiopia, FGM was often performed early, sometimes when children were only 7 days old.
Researchers found that people in that community believed that this would ensure that one day the girl would become a 'good wife' and also be obedient, rather than being a burden to her husband.
Many people believed that FGM made childbirth easier for women, but the truth is that it can complicate the birthing process.
In Kenya, FGM was traditionally seen as a rite of passage marking a girl's transition into womanhood, and it was often performed during the early stages of adolescence, like a ceremony.

However, in some cases, it was found that girls could undergo FGM at the age of 8, and many girls ended up becoming pregnant while still teenagers, because they were considered mature enough and capable of engaging in sexual activity after FGM.
Researchers state that their findings indicate that there are many different reasons why FGM is still practiced.
As laws and public opinions change, the way it is done and the place where it is done also change.
For example, parents may attempt to do it strictly even though it is illegal, because they believe it is necessary for their daughter to have a good life or to find a good husband.
It should be noted that because FGM is illegal in some areas, researching it can be challenging, and people may not provide accurate responses on the matter.

Researchers suggest that in the future, in addition to enforcement, governments and health organizations should aim to end FGM by addressing the misconceptions people have about the practice and educating them about its dangers.

This research was conducted by a consortium of scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and is part of a larger project called the 'Yes I Do programme', which aims to reduce the number of teenage pregnancies, child marriages, and FGM.

Hormonal imbalance, germ cell apoptosis, defective spermatogenesis, and morphological changes in the testes of the African giant pouched rat (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) following exposure to sodium metavanadate.
The world has recently experienced an increase in vanadium levels.
This device is known as a hazardous object.
This study was conducted with the aim of investigating the effects of sodium metavanadate (SMV) on the fertility of albino mice.
The SMV compound was administered to mice orally every day for 14 consecutive days at a dose of 3 mg/kg of body weight.
The packaged water used for injections was sterilized by an autoclave.
We examined the germ cells present in the testis, their storage structures and quality, as well as changes in the morphology of the sperm after administering the SMV compound to mice.
Our findings showed that the AGR group treated with SMV had increased progesterone levels, while testosterone, FSH, and LH levels decreased.
Moreover, the group treated with the SMV compound showed an increase in tumor progression due to the proliferation of defective tumor types as well as the rise of the P53 immunopositive cell.

The examination of the testicular structure revealed the presence of a germinal and Sertoli cell layer responsible for spermatogenesis; additionally, the thickening of the basement membrane was observed along with the presence of a lumen.
There was a weakening of the collagen fibers, damage and weakening of the bone marrow, as well as the death of Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells.

In summary, when SMV compound is administered in small doses, it severely affects reproductive hormones, significantly reduces the quantity and quality of stored sperm, and causes changes that can destroy or weaken Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells, potentially leading to infertility.
Researchers state that pollutants found in contaminated air cause bone loss in mice.
Researchers discovered that the compound known as vanadium damages the bone structure of mice and their reproductive capacity (fertility).

Because this device is also hazardous to people, there is a proposal for further research to be conducted to determine whether this device, which is commonly found in our environment due to pollution, may pose certain risks to human health.
Although vanadium is a metal, it can enter the atmosphere in very small particles such as dust, for example, from oil and coal combustion.
As the world continues to use these fossil fuels, vanadium emissions increasingly pollute the air.
We know well that people in areas where it is present can contract diseases such as anemia, dryness of the skin and eyes, as well as chest pain.
Recently, scientists have also been interested in understanding the effect of vanadium on fertility.
They have started researching these substances using mice, which are often used in laboratories due to their similarity to humans.
In this research, scientists aimed to determine the effect of vanadium on a well-known mouse species found in West Africa, called the African spiny mouse.
They wanted to understand how vanadium affects the reproductive system of male mice, particularly their sperm, hormones, and the structure of their testes.
Researchers administered vanadium to six male mice once a day for 14 days.
At the same time, six other mice were given water as the "control" group in the experiment conducted.

Since the water was not expected to affect the mice, the researchers were to ensure that any changes observed in the first six mice would have resulted from the vanadium compound they were exposed to.
After 14 days, they examined whether the levels of hormones such as testosterone had changed, and they also observed their testes and counted their sperm.
Using the technique of transmission electron microscopy (TEM), they were able to observe all the structural changes that occurred in the seeds in detail, down to the individual bricks.
Researchers found that mice exposed to vanadium had significantly lower testosterone levels, along with other important reproductive hormones.
The mice that were exposed to vanadium had very low fertility, and their offspring were not healthy.
For example, researchers observed that some mouse embryos lacked a head or their tails were curled, and they also noted that they did not move as much as the embryos in mice that were given water.
Since sperm are the male reproductive cells used to fertilize the eggs in female organisms, these mutations made it difficult for these mice to reproduce.
Finally, the researchers found that some bricks in the mouse kidneys were severely damaged or sometimes completely destroyed by vanadium.
The researchers stated that the mutations they discovered could result in proteins with altered functions.
They stated that animals exposed to vanadium compounds and other pollutants may experience reproductive failure and could potentially become extinct due to these emissions.
Since humans are also classified as mammals like mice, scientists should therefore investigate the potential harm of vanadium in areas where it is prevalent to human health.

Researchers warned that some of the mutations they discovered in the animal species and their habitats were different from those identified in previous scientific studies, indicating a need for further research to understand the risks associated with vanadium compounds.

This research was conducted by scientists from Nigeria and Egypt in collaboration, and it adds to the existing knowledge of scientists on how animals, and sometimes humans, are affected by environmental degradation.
The Utilization of Indigenous Plant Species in the North West Ethiopia Region
The plants in the wetlands of Northwest Ethiopia in general, and in the Gozamin district in particular, have not been sufficiently studied.
The purpose of this research is to further understand the plants in the forest and their cultural significance.
The cluster sampling method was used based on the genetic differences of the selected samples.

The data collection was organized by dividing the area into four sections: the first section ranged from the farmer's house to 10 meters, the second section from 10 meters to 20 meters, the third section from 20 meters to 30 meters, and the fourth section from 30 meters to 40 meters, starting from the back of the farmer's house based on the size of the yard.
The questions with fill-in-the-blanks are asked to assess the respondent's knowledge about plant species.
A total of 238 plant species of cultural significance from 81 families were identified.
Of these, 39% were grassland, 29% were shrubland, and 6% were wetlands.
Perennial plants constituted the majority of the harvested plants (83%), while non-perennial plants made up the remaining portion (17%).
The Poaceae family had the most plant species, with 22, followed by Fabaceae with 21, and Asteraceae with 15.

Of the recorded plants, 140 (58.6%) were of ecological importance, 84 (35%) were food plants, 83 (34.7%) were medicinal, 39 (16.3%) were animal fodder, 57 (23.8%) were used for making artifacts, 60 (25%) were timber, 50 (21%) were used in human settings, and 1 (0.4%) was poisonous.
In the classification, it was discovered that Cordia Africana was an important plant in the region's culture and was at risk of extinction, followed by Ficus sur.
The primary importance of Cordia africana was in construction, while its secondary importance was in medicine.
The Sorensen similarity index for 64% of the surveyed locations did not exceed 0.5.
The results showed that household plants have many benefits and are long-lasting.
Food security and environmental conservation heavily rely on understanding the cultural practices of people related to the plants in their households.

The small similarities/different plant species in the region in the kebele indicated that there were significant differences in plant species. This was due to the diverse environmental conditions in the kebele.
The fields in Ethiopia enable food production and preserve the environment.
Researchers state that many Ethiopians cultivate food crops, flowers, medicinal plants, and animal feed, either under shade or in enclosures in their farms.
Research these fields to assess their benefits in ensuring food security and contributing to environmental conservation.
People around the world cultivate plants for food, to earn money, and for other cultural benefits.
Fields also preserve important plant species that are either rare or endangered in other regions.
In Ethiopia, not much research has been conducted on what exactly people cultivate in their fields.
In this study, the researchers aimed to investigate the plants that people in the Gozamin district, in North West Ethiopia, cultivate in their fields and what they use them for.
They discovered and counted plants in 357 fields in that area.
They also asked people in the area about what they used those plants for.
Researchers discovered that all the farms in Gozamin were less than a hectare in size.
They collected and identified 238 different plant species.
The majority of the plants (83%) were perennial, while a few (17%) were annual.
The findings showed that they used plants for food, medicine, construction, animal feed, and other cultural benefits.
Most plants have more than one benefit.
For example, the broad-leaved tree from the North can be used as medicine, flowers, animal feed, shade, fencing, and other cultural benefits.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for ecological purposes such as making fences, boundaries, shade, and flowers.
The researchers stated that this helped in preserving the environment.
Plants that form barriers also helped protect the crops.
Slightly more than one-third (35%) of the plants were harvested for consumption, such as fruits, vegetables, seeds, and spices.
However, they said that the fields in this area mostly yielded crops.

Researchers stated that about 35% of the plants were used as traditional medicine for humans and animals, while about 21% were used for religious and spiritual purposes, fumigation, fragrance, and cooking.
Some plants (17%) were used to feed cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
The remaining 24% was used in construction, manufacturing agricultural tools, weaving, and making crafts.
Since most people in rural areas used firewood, 25% of the plants were used as firewood.
The researchers stated that one plant species (0.4%) was reported to have been used for poisoning.
They also stated that the distribution of plants in the area had an impact on the environment, the food preferences of people, as well as the economic conditions of households and business needs.
For example, the area called Wenka, which had irrigation water and was near a major town, had many farms and contained 130 different plant species.
The people of Wenka also farmed and sold crops and vegetables in the city market.
Finally, the researchers stated that most farmers preferred to cultivate crops with multiple benefits.
The researchers stated that their findings confirmed that indeed farmers cultivated different types of crops in their fields, and for various reasons.
Although these researchers discovered that most farmers cultivated medicinal plants, other researchers stated that trees were more commonly found in this area.
The researchers of this study were based in universities in Ethiopia.
